deep.reconstruction:
This is a printed page of an 18th-century German algebra textbook, p. 96, §§186-188, with handwritten marginalia at the right edge that are cut off. The printed text is not Gauss's. The marginalia are the start of a numerical computation that continues on the next page.

(a) End of §186, continuing Example 3 from p.95. The problem is x+y=6, xy=1. The text remarks that x and y are the two roots of one quadratic. Substituting y=1/x into x+y=6 gives x^2-6x+1=0, whose roots are x=3±2√2.

(b) §187, the solution of the depressed cubic x^3 = f x + g.
- Put x=a+b. Then x^3 = a^3+b^3+3ab(a+b) = a^3+b^3+3ab·x.
- Set p=a^3 and q=b^3, so ab = (pq)^(1/3). This gives x^3 = p+q+3(pq)^(1/3)·x.
- Compare coefficients with x^3=fx+g: 3(pq)^(1/3)=f and p+q=g.
- Hence 27pq=f^3, i.e. pq=f^3/27 and 4pq=4f^3/27.
- Also g^2=(p+q)^2=p^2+2pq+q^2. Subtracting 4pq gives (p-q)^2 = g^2-(4/27)f^3, so p-q = √(g^2-4f^3/27).
- With p+q=g: p = (g+√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2 and q = (g-√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2.
- So x = ∛p + ∛q = ∛[(g+√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2] + ∛[(g-√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2].
- In modern form, with x^3+Px+Q=0 (P=-f, Q=-g): x = ∛(-Q/2+√(Q^2/4+P^3/27)) + ∛(-Q/2-√(Q^2/4+P^3/27)).

Example: x^3=6x+9, so f=6, g=9.
- g^2=81 and (4/27)·216=32, so √(81-32)=7.
- x = ∛(16/2) + ∛(2/2) = ∛8 + ∛1 = 2+1 = 3.
- Check: 27 = 18+9. My addition: x^3-6x-9 = (x-3)(x^2+3x+3), so the other two roots, (-3±i√3)/2, are complex.

The Anmerkung names this 'Cardan's or Scipione del Ferro's rule'.

(c) §188, Lehrsatz (the factor theorem). Let the equation be monic, ordered and brought to zero. If x=a makes it vanish, then a is a root and x-a is a factor; the cofactor Q has degree one less. The proof starts with Q·(x-a)=Qx-Qa=0 and argues that some factor must vanish. It breaks off at the page turn.

(d) Gauss's marginalia, partly cut off: 13, 1296, 4000, 7205., 396302., 3697., 721., 14, ., 738., 369(2)., and at the bottom √(0,6 √0,…) and ⁴√.
- These are the opening of a digit-by-digit square-root extraction of √13, carried out at length on the next page. There it yields √13 ≈ 3.605551275463989293119235.
- Reading of the steps: 1296=36^2, leaving remainder 4 → 400 → 4000. Trial divisor 720, then 7205·5. Then 72055·55=3963025, i.e. the next digit pair of 3.6055… is processed. Then 72110…, i.e. twice 36055, and so on.
- The bottom marginalia √(0,6√0,2) equals ⁴√(36/500) = ⁴√0.072 ≈ 0.518, as written on the next page.
- The next page relates this to high-precision natural logarithms. ln(10^5)=11.51292546…, and ln(0.3+√0.05) = ln((3+√5)/10) = ln(φ^2/10) ≈ -0.6470142262.
- None of this is connected to the printed mathematics of the page; the margin is used as scratch space.
errors: Printed §187: taking √(g^2-4f^3/27)=p-q chooses one sign of the square root. This is harmless because p and q are symmetric. More seriously, the cube roots must be chosen so that ∛p·∛q = f/3. The text does not say this, and it matters when complex values arise (casus irreducibilis, g^2 < 4f^3/27). The text is silent on that case and on the other two roots.
Printed example: correct (x=3). 'eine Wurzel' rightly signals that only one root is obtained; the other two are complex.

Printed §188 proof (as far as visible): the argument 'Q(x-a)=Qx-Qa=0, so one factor must vanish' presupposes the factorization it is meant to prove. The proof is not rigorous by modern standards (it should use polynomial division with remainder f(x)-f(a) divisible by x-a). It is truncated at the page break.
Previous page (p.95, not this page): y=3-3√2 is a misprint for 3-2√2; this page's quadratic x^2-6x+1=0 confirms 3±2√2.
Next-page context: the √13 value 3.605551275463989293119235 agrees with the true value 3.6055512754639892931192212674… to about 22 decimals; the last digits differ (…235 vs …2213).

results.what: Solution of the depressed cubic x^3=fx+g via x=a+b, giving x=∛((g+√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2)+∛((g-√(g^2-4f^3/27))/2)
results.modern_name: Cardano's formula (del Ferro–Tartaglia–Cardano solution of the cubic)
results.usually_credited_to: Scipione del Ferro (c.1515), Tartaglia (1535), published by Cardano in Ars Magna (1545)

results.what: Root a of a monic polynomial implies (x-a) is a factor with a cofactor of degree n-1
Two numbers with given sum and product are the roots of a quadratic (x^2-6x+1=0)
Gauss's marginal digit-by-digit extraction of √13 (continued on next page to ~24 decimals), plus a note √(0.6√0.2)=⁴√(36/500)
results.modern_name: Long-hand square root extraction; high-precision numerical computation

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed textbook page with standard material (Cardano's formula, factor theorem). Gauss's only contribution is marginal scratch work for a high-precision square root of 13. His habit of extensive numerical calculation is well known.

checkable.asserts: equals (x-3)*(x**2+3*x+3); the other roots are complex
roots 3-2*sqrt(2), 3+2*sqrt(2), so p.95's '3-3√2' is a misprint
marginal step in square-root extraction of √13

transcription_corrections: Printed text transcription is essentially correct; the cube-root index 3 above each √ in §187 is correctly rendered as ∛.

Margin: entries read in the image as '13 / 1296 / 4000 / 7205. / 396302. / 3697. / 721. / 14 / . / 738. / 369(2).', truncated at the binding/edge. The full version on the next page is 13, 1296, 4000, 72055, 3963025, 36975, 72110512, ...; they are square-root-of-13 extraction steps.
Bottom margin '√(0,6 √0,…' and '⁴√' correspond to √(0,6√0,2) and ⁴√(36/500) on the next page, not '√0,6 √0'.
